newsitem.title: UK: IBCA rates MBNA Int'l Bank SPV notes AAA l-term.
newsitem.headline: IBCA rates MBNA Int'l Bank SPV notes AAA l-term.

text.p: IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said on Friday it assigned a long-term rating of AAA to 240 million stg of senior notes issued via a special purpose vehicle, Chester Asset Receivables Dealings No 3 Ltd.

At the same time, a long-term rating of A plus is assigned to 10 million stg of subordinated certificates issued via a second special purpose vehicle, Credit Card Securitisation International Limited, which was privately placed, IBCA said in a statement.

IBCA said MBNA International Bank (MBNAIB) specialises in credit card originations and is using securitisation as the primary funding source. This is MBNAIB's third series, bringing the total volume of its securitisation to 707 million stg, IBCA said.
MBNAIB is the wholly owned UK subsidiary of MBNA America Bank, N.A. and is also the first issuer to securitise sterling credit card receivables, IBCA said.
It is rated A long-term and A1 short-term by IBCA; MBNA America Bank, N.A. is rated AA minus long-term and A1 plus short-term.
"Today's announcement marks IBCA's entry into the asset backed credit card ratings market," IBCA said.

"In evaluating the issue the agency considered the following factors: the quality of the collateral; experience of MBNAIB as a servicer; the amount of credit enhancement in the form of excess spread and a 10 percent cash collateral account (CCA); and a rapid amortisation mechanism," IBCA said.
"The credit card portfolio of MBNA America Bank, N.A. has experienced consistently better-than-average losses compared to its industry peers in the U.S," IBCA said.

"IBCA expects the credit card receivables originated by MBNAIB to perform better than the U.S. credit card industry because it is unlikely for personal bankruptcies in the U.K. to reach the same level as those in the U.S. during the term of the transaction," IBCA said.
"Losses due to personal bankruptcies comprise nearly 50 percent of credit card losses in the U.S. but are likely to be very small in the U.K," IBCA said.
